{{short description|American biologist}}
'''Harold Francis Greeney III''' (born 1972) is an American biologist best known for establishing the [http://www.yanayacu.org Yanayacu Biological Research Station and Center for Creative Studies] on the eastern slopes of [[Antisana|Antisana volcano]] in [[Ecuador]]. He received his PhD from the Department of Behavioural Ecology, [[University of Wrocław]], Wrocław, Poland in 2008, his MSc from Department of Entomology at [[the University of Arizona]] in 1999, and his BSc at [[Wake Forest University]] in 1993.

He is an author on over 500 peer-reviewed biological research articles concerning the ecology, behavior, and evolution of invertebrate and vertebrate species.<ref>{{cite web | title=Harold GREENEY &#124; Owner, Research Director &#124; PhD &#124; Research profile | url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Harold-Greeney?ev=hdr_xprf }}</ref> Greeney's work on the reproductive biology of neotropical birds resulted in a Pamela and Alexander F. Skutch Research Award by the [[Association of Field Ornithologists]] in 2005, and a John Simon Guggenheim Fellowship in 2015 <ref>{{cite web | title=Guggenheim Fellowships: Supporting Artists, Scholars, & Scientists | url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/harold-f-greeney }}</ref>.  Although he has published information on the nesting behavior of more than 700 species of birds, Greeney is well known for his interest in [[antpitta]]s, about which he published an authoritative book in 2018 <ref>{{cite web | title=Antpittas and Gnateaters | url=https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/antpittas-and-gnateaters-9781472919656/ }}</ref>.

His passion and skill for finding bird nests, especially of rare or difficult to find species, have led to Greeney's participation in several nature documentaries such as [https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/hummingbirds-magic-in-the-air-introduction/5424/ ''Hummingbirds: Magic in the Air''], [https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/an-original-duckumentary-preview/7957/ ''An Original DUCKumentary''], and Hummingbirds: Jewelled Messengers, as either a scientific consultant or in an on-air role <ref>https://www.imdb.com/name/nm7267316/</ref>.

Along with a group of North American collaborators, Greeney has maintained an active [[National Science Foundation|NSF]]-funded research program entitled Collaborative Research: Caterpillars and Parasitoids in the Andes of Eastern Ecuador<ref>{{cite web|title=NSF Awards|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/piSearch.do?SearchType=piSearch&page=1&QueryText=yanayacu&PIFirstName=&PILastName=&PIInstitution=&PIState=&PIZip=&PICountry=&Restriction=0&Search=Search|publisher=National Science Foundation}}</ref> since 2004.

Greeney has three children.
